question: Arely controls a [Barony Vampire]. Nico controls a [Trained Jackal]. Arely casts [Prey Upon], targeting the Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal. In response, Nico casts [Hanabi Blast], targeting the Barony Vampire. What happens?
answer:
Hanabi Blast resolves first (last in, first out), dealing 2 damage to Barony Vampire. Since Barony Vampire is a 3/2, 2 damage is lethal, and it's destroyed as a state-based action and put into Arely's graveyard before Nico gets priority again. Hanabi Blast then returns to its owner's hand (Nico's hand), and Nico discards a card at random. When Prey Upon then resolves, it checks its targets: Barony Vampire is no longer on the battlefield (it left the zone it was in when targeted), so it is now an illegal target under rule 608.2b, while Trained Jackal is still a legal target. Because not *all* of Prey Upon's targets are illegal, the spell doesn't get countered on resolution and still resolves, but per the Prey Upon ruling, if either target is illegal as it resolves, no creature deals or is dealt damage. So the 'fight' simply fizzles for damage purposes — Trained Jackal takes no damage and deals none.

Step-by-step: (1) Arely casts Prey Upon targeting Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal; it goes on the stack. (2) In response, Nico casts Hanabi Blast targeting Barony Vampire; per rule 117.7, Hanabi Blast is on top of the stack and resolves first. (3) Hanabi Blast deals 2 damage to Barony Vampire, then returns to Nico's hand, then Nico discards a random card (Hanabi Blast ruling #0 clarifies the owner is the one who discards/receives it back). (4) State-based actions destroy Barony Vampire (2 damage ≥ 2 toughness) before either player gets priority again. (5) Prey Upon resolves: it checks targets per rule 608.2b — Barony Vampire is illegal (no longer in the battlefield zone it was targeted in), Trained Jackal is still legal. Since not both targets are illegal, Prey Upon resolves but, per the Prey Upon ruling, causes no damage to be dealt by or to any creature, since Trained Jackal has no legal partner to fight.

End result: Barony Vampire is dead in Arely's graveyard (killed by Hanabi Blast, not by the fight), Trained Jackal is completely unharmed, Hanabi Blast is back in Nico's hand, and Nico has discarded one random card.

This assumes state-based actions are checked (destroying Barony Vampire) before Prey Upon resolves, which is required since state-based actions are performed before any player receives priority again after Hanabi Blast finishes resolving — there's no other plausible timing here.

question: Annabel controls [Altar of Dementia] and casts [Too Greedily, Too Deep] returning Nolan's [Sepulchral Primordial] to the battlefield. Can Annabel use Altar of Dementia to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial and return it to the battlefield using its own triggered ability?
answer:
No. Once Too Greedily, Too Deep finishes resolving (putting Sepulchral Primordial onto the battlefield under Annabel's control, then dealing damage equal to its power to each other creature), Sepulchral Primordial's own "when this creature enters" ability triggers. This is an enters-the-battlefield trigger, which rule [603.6] identifies as a zone-change trigger; the most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Assuming the standard sequence — the triggered ability is put on the stack (with its target for each opponent's graveyard chosen) as soon as the spell finishes resolving, before Annabel gets priority to do anything else — Sepulchral Primordial is still sitting on the battlefield at that moment, not in any graveyard. It therefore cannot be a legal target for its own "put up to one target creature card from that player's graveyard onto the battlefield" ability at the time targets are locked in. Only after that trigger is already on the stack (with its target already fixed) does Annabel get priority to activate Altar of Dementia and sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial. Doing so sends Sepulchral Primordial to Nolan's graveyard (its owner), and under rule [400.7] it becomes a brand-new object with no connection to the permanent that just left the battlefield — but this is irrelevant to the already-stacked trigger, because that trigger's target was chosen earlier and can't be changed to point at Sepulchral Primordial now. So the sacrifice happens one step too late: it can feed Altar of Dementia's own effect ("Target player mills cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power," per Altar of Dementia's text) to mill Nolan for Sepulchral Primordial's power, but it cannot cause Sepulchral Primordial's own triggered ability to bring itself back. If instead targets for a triggered ability were chosen only when the ability resolves rather than when it's put on the stack, this loop could work — but that is not how the timing goes here, and this reasoning assumes the normal case where the trigger's target is set immediately after Too Greedily, Too Deep finishes resolving and before any player receives priority. This holds the same whether there are two players or more: Sepulchral Primordial's ability triggers "for each opponent" and picks a target from each opponent's graveyard separately at that same moment, so in a multiplayer game only the portion of the trigger aimed at Nolan's graveyard is even relevant, and it faces the identical timing problem.

question: Ari casts [Memories Returning]. Does Noor have a chance to exile it with [Dawnhand Dissident] before Ari can cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost?
answer:
No — Noor does not get an automatic chance to exile Memories Returning with Dawnhand Dissident before Ari re-casts it via flashback, because the ruling on Memories Returning explicitly says that if the card is put into your graveyard during your own turn, you can cast it with flashback "before any other player can take any actions" ([Memories Returning ruling #2]).

Here's why: Memories Returning is a sorcery, so it can only be cast during a main phase with an empty stack and priority ([117.1a]). Ari casts it, it resolves and goes to Ari's graveyard (it is only exiled instead of going to the graveyard if the flashback cost was the one paid to cast it — see [Memories Returning ruling #4], [702.34a]). Since Ari cast it for its normal mana cost {2}{U}{U} the first time, it lands in the graveyard as a normal sorcery card once it resolves ([608.1]).

Dawnhand Dissident's second ability, "{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard," is an activated ability, and only a player with priority may activate it ([117.1a]). Noor cannot target Memories Returning with that ability while it's still a spell on the stack — it has to actually be sitting in the graveyard first, because the ability's target is "a card from a graveyard," and a spell on the stack is not a card in a graveyard ([112.1]).

The official ruling on Memories Returning tells you exactly how the timing shakes out: once the card is in Ari's graveyard on Ari's own turn, Ari is entitled to cast it again with flashback before any other player, including Noor, gets to take any action ([Memories Returning ruling #2]). So as long as Ari immediately casts the flashback copy (paying {7}{U}{U} instead of the mana cost, per [Memories Returning ruling #4]) the moment they're able to, Noor never gets a window to activate Dawnhand Dissident against it.

The one caveat: this protection only applies if Ari actually takes the flashback-cast action right away. If Ari instead passes priority (or is somehow prevented from immediately re-casting), then priority would pass to Noor in turn, and at that point Noor could activate Dawnhand Dissident's "{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard" ability targeting Memories Returning while it's sitting in the graveyard, which would exile it and make it impossible for Ari to flashback it afterward. So the outcome hinges on Ari acting on their guaranteed first opportunity rather than passing priority first.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No. Once Arely casts Flash Conscription and gains control of Coral Commando, Coral Commando's controller changes, and rule [506.4a] states that a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes. A creature removed from combat immediately stops being an attacking creature ([506.4], [506.4a]). So Coral Commando is no longer attacking after Flash Conscription resolves — it becomes an untapped, hasty creature under Arely's control for the rest of the turn, but it will not deal combat damage as an attacker and does not become a new attacking or blocking creature on its own.

This is true regardless of the 2HG format: the rule that a controller change removes a permanent from combat ([506.4a]) is a general combat rule that isn't altered by the Two-Headed Giant team-turn structure. (If your table were using the optional 'shared team turns' variant described in [805.10b], attackers are still declared the same way under [508.1]/[508.1k], and a mid-combat controller change would still remove the creature from combat under the same [506.4a] rule — so the outcome doesn't change between a normal two-team 2HG game and the shared-team-turns variant.)

One timing note: this assumes Flash Conscription resolves after Coral Commando has already been declared as an attacker (as the question states). If instead control changed before attackers were declared, Coral Commando simply couldn't have been declared as an attacker by Aubrey at all, since Aubrey wouldn't control it at that time.

question: Axel controls [Vastwood Gorger] and attacks Nico's [Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset]. Before damage is dealt, Nico activates [Barrin, Master Wizard], sacrificing Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset. Does Vastwood Gorger deal damage? If so, to what?
answer:
Vastwood Gorger deals no combat damage at all. Sacrificing Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset removes it from the battlefield, which removes it from combat under rule [506.4c]. Since Vastwood Gorger was attacking Teferi specifically (a planeswalker, not a player), removing Teferi from combat does not remove Vastwood Gorger from combat — it remains an attacking creature, but it is no longer attacking any player, planeswalker, or battle, per [506.4c]. Vastwood Gorger has no trample or trample-over-planeswalkers ability (it's a vanilla 5/6 per its printed text), so the exception in [702.19e] for trample-over-planeswalkers creatures does not apply, and [702.19f] confirms that without that ability none of its damage can ever be redirected to the defending player even though the planeswalker it was attacking is gone. Under the combat damage assignment rules in [510.1b], an unblocked creature that isn't currently attacking anything (for example because what it was attacking left the battlefield) assigns no combat damage. So Vastwood Gorger simply deals zero damage this combat; it doesn't hit Nico, and it isn't redirected anywhere.

Note on timing: this assumes Barrin's activated ability resolves and Teferi is sacrificed before the combat damage step (i.e., 'before damage is dealt' as stated), so the removal-from-combat rules apply before damage assignment. If instead Teferi had already been removed after damage was already assigned/dealt, the outcome wouldn't change here since no damage was assigned yet in the scenario described.
